slides.sub: The families you came from, the household you are forming
slides.title: Room 3: Family and Boundaries
slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson 8. This room is about the families you came from, and the household you are forming.

slides.quote: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
slides.narration:
Let’s begin with Scripture. Genesis chapter 2, verse 24.

“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”

slides.title: Leave. Hold fast. Become one.
body: One of the earliest statements about marriage in the Bible: a movement with three steps.
slides.narration:
This is one of the earliest statements about marriage in the Bible. It comes at the very beginning, in the account of creation, and it describes a movement with three steps. Leave. Hold fast. Become one.

Let’s take the first two carefully.

slides.title: Not to abandon
body: Honouring father and mother remains a command. Marriage creates a new covenant loyalty: the couple learns to make decisions together.
slides.note: This is the pattern of marriage, not how every household in every culture must be arranged.
slides.narration:
To “leave” does not mean to stop loving your parents, or to abandon them. Scripture is clear elsewhere that honouring father and mother remains a command, and honour includes practical care. Jesus himself rebuked people who used religious excuses to avoid caring for their parents. Marriage creates a new covenant loyalty. The couple must learn to make decisions together, even when they remain closely connected to their wider families.

One more caution. This verse is a statement about the pattern of marriage. It is not a description of how every household in every culture must be arranged. Many families live close together, or in the same home, across generations, and that is not wrong. The principle holds in every setting: the married couple learns to decide together.

slides.title: Put them in the right order
body: You can honour your parents and still leave them. You can hold fast to your spouse and still love your family.
slides.sub: Extended family is loved without being allowed to govern.
slides.narration:
So here is the truth this lesson stands on. You can honour your parents and still leave them. You can hold fast to your spouse and still love your family. The Bible does not ask you to choose between them. It asks you to put them in the right order.

Honour your parents. Leave your parents. Hold fast to your spouse. Build a marriage where extended family is loved without being allowed to govern it.

body: “I love you enough to have an honest relationship with you, and I will not let this relationship run our marriage.”
slides.narration: A boundary, then, is not rejection. Often it is the opposite. It says, “I love you enough to have an honest relationship with you, and I will not let this relationship run our marriage.” You may support your parents financially while still making household decisions together. You can visit often without letting them govern your marriage. You can disagree with them respectfully and remain a son or daughter who honours them.

slides.kicker: Here is how it goes wrong
slides.title: Feelings, not arrangements
body: “I love my parents.” “My family is very important to me.” Both true. Neither answers a practical question.
slides.narration:
Here is how it usually goes wrong.

A couple can genuinely love their parents, mean well in every direction, and still create serious problems, because they have never clarified how their responsibilities to their families change when a new household begins. They talk about their families in terms of feeling rather than arrangement. “I love my parents.” “My family is very important to me.” Both true. Neither answers a single practical question.

list: Who makes decisions about your home?
How often will parents visit? Can one stay indefinitely?
How much money will you provide?
What happens when a parent criticises your spouse?
When your spouse and parents disagree, whose expectations govern your marriage?
slides.narration: Who makes decisions about your home? How often will parents visit? Can a parent stay indefinitely? How much money will you provide? What happens when one of them criticises your spouse? And the one underneath all the others: when your spouse and your parents disagree, whose expectations will govern the decisions of your marriage, and how will you respond honourably?

slides.title: “That’s my mother”
body: One mother visits whenever she likes. The other expects notice. Neither has said so.
slides.sub: The other partner hears: “My mother’s comfort matters more than yours.”
slides.narration:
Here is a common scene. One partner’s mother expects to visit whenever she likes, because that is how the family has always worked. The other expects visits to be arranged in advance, because that is how theirs has worked. Neither has ever said so, because to each of them, that is simply how families behave. Then they are married, and it happens, and one says, “That’s my mother. You can’t tell her she needs permission to come to her son’s house.” And what the other hears is, “My mother’s comfort matters more than yours.”

They now appear to be arguing about a visit. They are not. They are arguing about something far larger: are we a married couple who decides things together, or are you still operating primarily as your parents’ child?

slides.title: Resentment goes the wrong way
body: Someone feels any boundary with a parent is betrayal, and expects their spouse to absorb the consequences. Resentment builds toward the spouse, not the parent.
slides.narration: And there is a second failure: loyalty conflict. Someone feels that setting any boundary with a parent is betrayal. So they will not say no to their family, and expect their spouse to absorb the consequences quietly. Resentment builds fast, and it builds toward the spouse, not the parent, which is precisely backwards.

slides.title: Where might loyalty to your family make it difficult for you to form your own household?
body: Take a moment before you go on.
slides.narration: Pause here. Where might loyalty to your family make it difficult for you to form your own household? Take a moment before you go on.

slides.title: Verses as ammunition
body: “Honour your father and mother” does not mean parents keep authority over you permanently. A loyalty contest with verses is what Lesson 2 forbids.
slides.narration: There is also a trap for Christians. “Honour your father and mother” is sometimes treated as though it means parents keep authority over you permanently. That is not what the Bible teaches about marriage. And the danger comes when Scripture is used as leverage. One says, “My mother is my mother. The Bible says I have to honour her.” The other replies, “I’m your spouse. You’re supposed to choose me.” Now you are in a loyalty contest with verses as ammunition, which is exactly what our rule in Lesson 2 forbids.

body: Not “Do you like my family?” but: what boundaries will protect our marriage while we continue to love our families well?
slides.narration: The question before the wedding is not “Do you like my family?” It is: what boundaries will protect our marriage while we continue to love our families well?

chips: What may be shared about disagreements
slides.narration: So be practical. Six questions are at the heart of this conversation.

list: Visits: how often, and can family visit without checking with both of us?
Money: what do we each owe our parents, and what is the actual figure?
Significant days: where do we spend the celebrations that matter most?
slides.narration:
First, visits and notice. How often will we see each set of parents, and can family visit without checking with both of us first?

Second, financial support. What financial responsibility do we each have toward our parents, and what is the actual figure?

Third, significant days. Where do we spend the holidays and celebrations that matter most?

slides.title: What may be shared about disagreements
body: Once parents become the place where every conflict is reported, you forgive each other and they go on carrying the offence.
slides.note: Privacy should protect your relationship, not isolate either person. Nothing prevents seeking confidential pastoral, professional or safety support.
slides.narration: Fourth, what may be shared about disagreements. When we disagree with each other, what can I tell my parents? That matters more than couples expect. Once parents become the place where every marital conflict gets reported, something unfortunate happens: the two of you forgive each other, and your parents go on carrying the offence. Your mother will still be angry about something you resolved months ago. But hear this clearly: privacy should protect your relationship, not isolate either person. No agreement prevents either of you from seeking confidential pastoral, professional or safety support.

list: When one of my parents criticises you, what do we do?
Who speaks to their own parents when a boundary needs setting?
slides.sub: Where safe and practical, each takes responsibility for their own relatives.
slides.narration:
Fifth, criticism. What do we do when one of my parents criticises you?

Sixth, who communicates a boundary. Who speaks to their own parents when a boundary needs setting? Where it is safe and practical, each of you should take responsibility for communicating boundaries to your own relatives. The point is not to leave one partner alone to absorb hostility.

body: When our families’ expectations conflict with decisions we have made together, how will we decide faithfully and communicate it with kindness?
slides.sub: You cannot keep everyone comfortable all the time.
slides.narration:
If you have time, there is one more question, and it is an honest one: when our families’ expectations conflict with decisions we have made together, how will we decide faithfully what to do, and how will we communicate it with kindness? You cannot keep everyone comfortable all the time.

There are other questions, such as keys, how long a parent may stay, and who decides when a parent needs money. Return to them when they become relevant.

list: Financial support for parents: name the actual amount.
One set of parents does not accept the marriage.
A decision that needs a parent’s approval.
An ageing parent who will need care.
slides.note: Respect cultural differences, but do not use them to excuse intrusion, isolation or control.
slides.narration: Some differences deserve extra care. Financial support for parents is one of the most serious differences in Christian marriages, and it is rarely only about money. It touches culture, duty and what a good son or daughter owes. Name the actual amount and the actual expectation, and do not resolve it in one evening. If one set of parents does not accept the marriage, it will not resolve itself after the wedding, and it should not be managed by the person they disapprove of. If one of you cannot presently make a significant decision without a parent’s approval, be honest about it now. It may be worth a conversation with someone outside both families. And if an ageing parent will need care, say so now and talk about what that will mean. Respect cultural differences, but do not use them to excuse intrusion, isolation or control.

slides.title: About twenty minutes
list: Where might loyalty to my family make it difficult for us to form our own household?
What did I grow up believing about parents and marriage?
What am I afraid of saying to my parents?
slides.narration: Your step has two parts. First, about twenty minutes alone with the questions in the worksheet. Where might loyalty to my family make it difficult for us to form our own household? What did I grow up believing about parents and marriage? What am I afraid of saying to my parents?

slides.title: 45 to 60 minutes
body: Work through the six main questions. Be specific. If you cannot answer one specifically, that is the discussion.
slides.narration: Then set aside 45 to 60 minutes, together, when neither of you is tired. Have your Lesson 2 rules in front of you. Work through the six main questions. Be specific. If you cannot answer a question specifically, that is the discussion.

body: Decide who will communicate it, and when you will review it. Record where you still disagree. Agreement is not required on everything today.
slides.narration: Then choose one boundary that will protect the household you are forming. Decide who will communicate it, and when you will review it. It might be about visits, about money, or about what is shared. And record where you still disagree. Agreement is not required on everything today.

body: Lord, thank You for the families that raised us. Help us honour them well. Teach us to leave, to hold fast, and to build a home that is faithful and free. Where we are afraid of disappointing someone, give us courage and kindness. Amen.
slides.narration:
Let me close with a short prayer.

Lord, thank You for the families that raised us. Help us honour them well. Teach us to leave, to hold fast, and to build a home that is faithful and free. Where we are afraid of disappointing someone, give us courage and kindness. Amen.
